title: The normal distribution: bell curves and probabilities
summary: Describe measurements with a mean and a spread, turn areas under the bell curve into probabilities, and check them by simulation.
license: Original work for Python Intelligence; license to be chosen by the owner

steps.title: How likely is a 186 cm adult?
steps.body:
Measure the height of thousands of adults and most land near the average, fewer further away, and very
few far away, in a symmetric bell shape. The same shape appears in measurement errors, test scores
and averages of many small effects. If you know just its centre and its spread, you can answer
questions like "what fraction of people are taller than 186 cm?" without counting anyone.

steps.title: Probability is area
steps.body:
For a continuous measurement, the chance of hitting one exact value is zero; what has a probability is
a **range**. The bell curve, called a **probability density**, is drawn so that the area under it
between two values is the probability of landing between them, and the whole area is 1. The
**normal (Gaussian) distribution** is the bell with centre `μ` (the mean) and width set by `σ` (the
standard deviation). Roughly 68% of values fall within one `σ` of the mean, 95% within two and 99.7%
within three.

questions: Can a probability density be larger than 1? (Think of a very narrow bell.)
If the mean height is 170 cm, what fraction of people are shorter than 170 cm?

steps.title: Watch a value become a z-score
steps.body: How many standard deviations above the mean is 186 cm, if `μ = 170` and `σ = 8`? Each frame shows the variables just before the highlighted line runs; the last frame shows what that line printed.

frames.note: Measure 186 cm against a mean of 170 and a spread of 8.
16 cm above the mean is two standard deviations.
Two standard deviations: only about 2.3% of values lie further above.

steps.title: The precise rules
steps.body:
**Density:** the normal distribution with mean `μ` and standard deviation `σ > 0` has density
`p(x) = exp(−(x − μ)² / (2σ²)) / (σ √(2π))`, highest at `x = μ` and symmetric about it.

**Cumulative probability:** `F(x) = P(X ≤ x)` is the area under the density to the left of `x`, so
`P(a < X ≤ b) = F(b) − F(a)`. For a continuous distribution the endpoints don't change the answer.

**In Python:** `statistics.NormalDist(mu, sigma)` gives `.pdf(x)`, `.cdf(x)` and `.inv_cdf(p)`, the
value below which a fraction `p` of the distribution lies (`0 < p < 1`).

**Simulation:** `random.Random(seed).gauss(mu, sigma)` draws normally distributed values; the same
seed gives the same sequence, and the fraction of draws in a range estimates its probability, more
closely the more draws you make.

steps.title: Run it: exact answers and a simulation
steps.body: Adult heights modelled as normal with `μ = 170` cm and `σ = 8` cm. Predict the first number before running.
steps.code:
import random
from statistics import NormalDist

heights = NormalDist(mu=170, sigma=8)
print(round(heights.cdf(178) - heights.cdf(162), 4))
print(round(1 - heights.cdf(186), 4))
print(round(heights.inv_cdf(0.9), 1))

rng = random.Random(7)
sample = [rng.gauss(170, 8) for _ in range(10_000)]
inside = sum(162 < h <= 178 for h in sample) / len(sample)
print(round(inside, 2))

steps.title: Your turn: the density from its formula
steps.body:
Complete `normal_pdf(x, mu, sigma)` from the formula above, using the `math` module. The checks compare
your values with `NormalDist(mu, sigma).pdf(x)`, which you can also call yourself to compare. Raise
`ValueError` if `sigma` is not positive.
hints: Compute `z = (x - mu) / sigma` first; the exponent is `-z * z / 2`.
Divide by `sigma * math.sqrt(2 * math.pi)` so the total area is 1.

tests.name: matches NormalDist
tests.code:
from statistics import NormalDist
for x, mu, sigma in ((0, 0, 1), (1.5, 0, 1), (-2, 0, 1), (186, 170, 8), (3, 5, 0.25), (-7.5, -6, 2.5)):
    got, want = normal_pdf(x, mu, sigma), NormalDist(mu, sigma).pdf(x)
    assert abs(got - want) <= 1e-12 * want, f'normal_pdf({x}, {mu}, {sigma}) should be about {want}; got {got}'

tests.name: the peak
tests.code:
import math
got = normal_pdf(10, 10, 2)
assert abs(got - 1 / (2 * math.sqrt(2 * math.pi))) < 1e-15, f'at the mean the density is 1 / (sigma * sqrt(2 pi)); got {got}'

tests.name: a narrow bell is taller than 1
tests.code:
got = normal_pdf(0, 0, 0.1)
assert got > 3.98 and abs(got - 3.989422804014327) < 1e-12, f'a density can exceed 1; got {got}'

tests.name: symmetric about the mean
tests.code: assert normal_pdf(4, 1, 2) == normal_pdf(-2, 1, 2), 'the same distance either side gives the same density'

tests.name: far from the mean
tests.code:
got = normal_pdf(30, 0, 1)
assert 0 <= got < 1e-190, f'thirty standard deviations away the density is tiny but not negative; got {got}'

tests.name: sigma must be positive

steps.title: Challenge: answer probability questions
steps.body:
Write three functions (raise `ValueError` whenever `sigma` is not positive):

- `prob_between(mu, sigma, a, b)`: the exact `P(a < X ≤ b)` with `NormalDist`; `0.0` when `a >= b`.
  `a` may be `-math.inf` and `b` may be `math.inf`.
- `value_at(mu, sigma, p)`: the value with a fraction `p` of the distribution below it; raise
  `ValueError` unless `0 < p < 1`.
- `estimate_between(mu, sigma, a, b, n, seed)`: the fraction of `n` draws that land in `a < x ≤ b`,
  drawing in order with one `random.Random(seed)` and its `.gauss(mu, sigma)`; raise `ValueError`
  if `n < 1`.
hints: For the estimate, make `rng = random.Random(seed)` once, then call `rng.gauss(mu, sigma)` `n` times, counting `a < x <= b`.

tests.name: exact probabilities
tests.code:
from statistics import NormalDist
d = NormalDist(170, 8)
for a, b in ((162, 178), (154, 186), (186, 300), (100, 170.5)):
    got, want = prob_between(170, 8, a, b), d.cdf(b) - d.cdf(a)
    assert abs(got - want) < 1e-15, f'prob_between(170, 8, {a}, {b}) should be {want}; got {got}'
assert abs(prob_between(0, 1, -1, 1) - 0.6826894921370859) < 1e-12

tests.name: open-ended ranges
tests.code:
import math
from statistics import NormalDist
assert abs(prob_between(0, 1, -math.inf, 1.5) - NormalDist().cdf(1.5)) < 1e-15, 'from minus infinity: just cdf(b)'
assert abs(prob_between(0, 1, 2, math.inf) - (1 - NormalDist().cdf(2))) < 1e-15, 'up to infinity: 1 - cdf(a)'
assert prob_between(5, 3, -math.inf, math.inf) == 1.0

tests.name: an empty range
tests.code: assert prob_between(0, 1, 2, 2) == 0.0 and prob_between(0, 1, 3, 1) == 0.0, 'a >= b gives 0.0'

tests.name: percentiles
tests.code:
from statistics import NormalDist
for mu, sigma, p in ((170, 8, 0.9), (0, 1, 0.5), (0, 1, 0.025), (-3, 0.5, 0.999)):
    got, want = value_at(mu, sigma, p), NormalDist(mu, sigma).inv_cdf(p)
    assert abs(got - want) < 1e-12, f'value_at({mu}, {sigma}, {p}) should be {want}; got {got}'

tests.name: p strictly between 0 and 1
the simulation recipe
tests.code:
import random
def reference(mu, sigma, a, b, n, seed):
    rng = random.Random(seed)
    return sum(a < rng.gauss(mu, sigma) <= b for _ in range(n)) / n
for args in ((170, 8, 162, 178, 2000, 7), (0, 1, -1, 1, 500, 1), (0, 1, 0, 100, 37, 3), (10, 2, 9, 9.5, 1000, 42)):
    got, want = estimate_between(*args), reference(*args)
    assert got == want, f'estimate_between{args}: draw n values in order from one random.Random(seed); expected {want}, got {got}'

tests.name: endpoints: above a, at most b
tests.code:
import random
rng = random.Random(5)
x = rng.gauss(0, 1)
none, every = estimate_between(0, 1, x, x + 1, 1, 5), estimate_between(0, 1, x - 1, x, 1, 5)
assert none == 0.0 and isinstance(none, float), f'a value equal to a is not inside a < x (and the result is the float 0.0); got {none!r}'
assert every == 1.0 and isinstance(every, float), f'a value equal to b is inside x <= b (and the result is the float 1.0); got {every!r}'

tests.name: empty or reversed ranges hold no draws
the estimate approaches the exact answer
tests.code:
exact = prob_between(0, 1, -1, 1)
est = estimate_between(0, 1, -1, 1, 20000, 11)
assert abs(est - exact) < 0.02 and isinstance(est, float), f'20,000 draws should land within 0.02 of {exact}; got {est}'

tests.name: bad input

questions.prompt: Test scores are normal with mean 60 and standard deviation 10. About what fraction score between 50 and 70?
questions.explanation: 50 to 70 is within one standard deviation of the mean.

questions.prompt: For a normal distribution with mean 0, what is `cdf(0)`?
questions.explanation: The distribution is symmetric about its mean, so half the area lies to the left.

questions.prompt: A density curve has the value 2.5 at some x. What does that tell you?
choices: The curve is narrow there: densities can exceed 1, only areas are probabilities
There is a 250% chance of x
questions.explanation: A density is probability per unit; a narrow bell is tall but its total area is still 1.

questions.prompt: How do you compute P(a < X ≤ b) from the cumulative function F?
questions.explanation: The area left of b minus the area left of a leaves the area between them.

steps.title: What you can do now
steps.body:
- Describe a normal distribution by its mean and standard deviation, and use the 68-95-99.7 rule.
- Explain why probabilities are areas under a density, and compute the density from its formula.
- Answer probability and percentile questions with `NormalDist`.
- Check an exact probability with a seeded simulation.
